extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology interested in ideas, perception, and the philosophy of mind
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from John Locke's Essay concerning Human Understanding setting out criteria and distinctions for how ideas are formed (sensation vs reflection), types of ideas and qualities, and what counts as perception. Useful for analyzing theories of mental representation and sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of Existence and Unity
rubrics_metrics.description: EXISTENCE and UNITY are ideas suggested to the understanding by every object without, and every idea within.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ideas are in our minds we consider them as being actually there (existence); whatever we can consider as one thing suggests to the understanding the idea of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of Power
rubrics_metrics.description: POWER is a simple idea received from sensation and reflection, formed by observing that we can act and that bodies produce effects in one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observing our own capacity to think and move and the causal effects of natural bodies yields the idea of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of Succession
rubrics_metrics.description: SUCCESSION is a simple idea arising from the constant train of ideas passing in the mind while awake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection on the continuous passing of ideas (one going and another coming) supplies the idea of succession more from the mind than from external objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple Ideas as the Materials of all Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple ideas, received only by sensation and reflection, are the materials out of which all other knowledge is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke challenges readers to name any simple idea not received by those two 'inlets'; he compares combinatorial power of few simple ideas to letters forming many words, and notes number/extension alone afford immense combinatorial possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive Ideas from Privative Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever in nature can, by affecting our senses, cause a perception in the mind produces a simple idea, even if the external cause is a privation of some quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include shadow (absence of light) producing a clear idea; some names (silence, invisible) denote negations rather than positive ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Ideas in the Mind from Causes in Things
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of sensations (e.g., heat/cold, light/darkness) are clear positive ideas in the mind, distinct from inquiries into the physical causes producing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical analysis should separate the idea-as-perception from the question of what in the external object produces it (a distinct inquiry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of Having Ideas without Knowing Physical Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: One may have clear ideas of sensible qualities without knowledge of their physical causes (painter/dyer example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clarity of an idea in the mind does not depend on the perceiver's scientific understanding of the cause in the external object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privative Causes can Produce Positive Ideas via Motions of Animal Spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: A privation in an external object can produce a positive idea in us because variations or abatements in the motions of animal spirits produce different sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke proposes a physiological hypothesis: different motions in the animal spirits (increase, decrease, variation) correspond to different ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Names Need Not Be Meaningless
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative terms (silence, invisible) often signify only the absence of certain ideas rather than a positive idea, but some privations produce definite positive perceptions (e.g., a shadow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between negative names with no positive idea and privative causes that nonetheless yield positive ideas when perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas in the Mind versus Qualities in Bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: What the mind perceives (IDEA) is different from the power in an object to produce that idea (QUALITY); ideas are perceptions in us, qualities are powers in external subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., a snowball has the power to produce ideas of white, cold, round in us (qualities), while the sensations themselves are ideas in the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary Qualities of Bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary (original) qualities in bodies that produce simple ideas are SOLIDITY, EXTENSION, MOTION or REST, NUMBER or FIGURE; these are inseparable from matter and persist under division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary qualities exist in objects whether perceived or not; Locke uses the grain-of-wheat division argument to show these qualities remain in parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodies Operate by Impulse (How Bodies Produce Ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies operate on one another by impulse and motion; it is impossible to conceive operation without contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since ideas are not united to external objects, some motion must be continued in our nerves or animal spirits to the seat of sensation to produce ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Qualities Produced by Insensible Particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of colours, smells, tastes, and sounds (secondary qualities) arise from the operation of insensible particles (different in figure, bulk, motion) on our senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke asks us to suppose minute particles whose differing motions and shapes cause the sensations we call colours, smells, tastes; God may annex particular ideas to particular motions without resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Qualities Depend on Primary Qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary qualities (colours, tastes, smells, sounds) are not real in bodies themselves but depend on primary qualities—bulk, figure, texture, and motion of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary qualities are powers to produce sensations and result from configurations of primary qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of Primary Qualities are Resemblances; Ideas of Secondary are Not
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of primary qualities resemble something really existing in bodies; ideas of secondary qualities do not resemble anything in the bodies themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because primary qualities (figure, motion, number) correspond to patterns in objects, their ideas are resemblances; secondary qualities are effects of powers and need not resemble their causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary Qualities Really Exist; Secondary Qualities Do Not Exist in Objects as Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular bulk, number, figure, and motion are really in bodies independent of perception; light, heat, whiteness, coldness are not really in them except as powers to produce sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sensation ceased (no eyes, ears, palate), colours/tastes/sounds would vanish, reducing to their causes—configurations of primary qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Qualities Exist Only as Modes or Powers of Primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary qualities exist in things only as ways in which primary qualities are modified to produce effects on other bodies (immediately or mediately perceivable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: porphyry's colours vanish without light; changes like blanching or melting are effects of powers, not qualities literally in the efficient body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explaining Relativity of Sensation (Warmth/Cold in Same Water)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same water may seem warm to one hand and cold to another because sensations depend on relative motion introduced into our nerves—an increase or diminution of motion in different hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a body's minute particles have more motion than one hand and less than the other, it can increase motion in one hand and decrease it in the other, producing different ideas (heat vs cold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three Sorts of Qualities in Bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities in bodies are of three sorts: (1) primary: bulk, figure, number, situation, motion/rest; (2) sensible: powers to produce ideas in us by operating on our senses; (3) powers to change other bodies' primary qualities so they produce different ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First are real/original qualities, second are powers resulting from primary qualities, third are powers affecting other bodies (sun melting wax). Locke elaborates how the second sort is commonly mistaken for real qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why Secondary Qualities are Mistaken for Real Qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: We mistake secondary qualities for real qualities because their ideas contain nothing of bulk, figure, or motion, and we fail to see how primary qualities could produce such ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we cannot perceive bulk/figure/motion in the production of colours or tastes, we infer a resemblance that isn't there; by contrast, when seeing one body change another (wax), we think the effect is a mere power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Qualities: Immediately vs Mediately Perceivable
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary qualities may be immediately perceivable (directly operating on our senses) or mediately perceivable (operating via changes they make in other bodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction helps classify how powers in objects lead to the ideas we have of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as the First Simple Idea of Reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: PERCEPTION is the first and simplest idea we have from reflection; it is sometimes called thinking in general, though perception is mostly passive while thinking implies some voluntary attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who have not reflected cannot be instructed into the idea of perception except by examining their own mental processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection Alone Gives the Idea of Perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Only by reflecting on what passes in our own minds (seeing, hearing, feeling, thinking) can we know what perception is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbal description alone cannot substitute for inner reflection to form the idea of perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception Requires that Organic Impression Reach the Mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception occurs only when impressions on the body reach the mind; impressions on organs that do not reach the mind produce no perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fire may burn a body with no perceptual effect if the motion does not continue to the brain; thus actual perception entails an idea being produced in the understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impulse on an Organ is Insufficient for Perception
rubrics_metrics.description: An impulse on a sensory organ may occur without perception if the mind does not take notice (attention) of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: while intently attending to thought, one may not perceive sounds though the ear receives normal impulses; perception requires the mind's observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Sensory Ideas in the Womb vs Innate Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Children may receive some ideas in the womb (hunger, warmth) by sensation but these are not innate principles; they are effects of bodily affections, not original characters impressed at constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke rejects the doctrine of innate ideas; prenatal sensations are contingent on external conditions and differ from claimed innate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception Often Altered by Judgment (Habituation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas received by sensation are frequently altered by the judgment through habitual experience, especially in vision where appearances are unconsciously converted into ideas of figure/space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sight presents a flat plane of varied shading, but by habitual judgment we interpret it as a convex globe; Locke supplies the blind-man-turned-sighted thought experiment (cube vs sphere) to illustrate that judgment, learned by experience, transforms raw sensation into recognized objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception vs Judgment are Easily Confused
rubrics_metrics.description: Because judgment can operate so quickly and habitually that it passes unnoticed, we often mistake ideas formed by judgment for direct perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke observes that many mental habituations perform actions without our noticing (covering eyes, by-words), so the mind's conversion of sensation into judged perception can be unconscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception Distinguishes Animals from Vegetables
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception sets animals apart from plants: though some plants exhibit motion, their changes are mechanical rather than sensations producing ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke treats perception as the hallmark of animal life and attributes various degrees of perception across animals appropriate to their condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception Present in Degrees Among Animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception exists in some degree in all animals, though the avenues and quickness vary; lesser creatures may have obscure and dull perception adapted to their needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The variety and gradation of perception across species reflects 'the wisdom and goodness of the Maker' in adapting faculties to creaturely states.
